            "description": "NIST CSF-NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a set of guidelines for mitigating organizational cybersecurity risks, published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) based on existing standards, guidelines, and practices.             "id": "1386",
            "name": "GDPR",
            "description": "The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a European Union regulation on information privacy in the European Union and the European Economic Area. The objective of the GDPR is to ensure the protection of personal information through a human rights-centric approach and allow secure transfer of personal information within and across jurisdictions. Effective from 25 May 2018, the GDPR imposes obligations onto organizations anywhere, so long as they target or collect data related to people in the EU.",

            "name": "ISO/IEC 27001:2022",
            "description": "ISO/IEC 27001 is the world's best-known standard for information security management systems (ISMS). It defines requirements an ISMS must meet. The ISO/IEC 27001 standard provides companies of any size and from all sectors of activity with guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an information security management system. Conformity with ISO/IEC 27001 means that an organization or business has put in place a system to manage risks related to the security of data owned or handled by the company, and that this system respects all the best practices and principles enshrined in this International Standard.",

            "name": "CDMC",
            "description": "Cloud Data Management Capabilities (CDMC) is a framework of best practices for companies that are migrating to or adopting cloud services. The framework enables organizations to securely migrate to cloud/hybrid cloud or multi-cloud environments, better protect their sensitive data, and leverage automation for improved cloud data management. It lays out how companies can establish clear accountability, controls, and governance around the broad spectrum of data and assets that exists within their cloud infrastructure.",

            "id": "1628",
            "name": "CCPA",
            "description": "The California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (CCPA) is the first US state comprehensive privacy law. CCPA gives consumers certain rights over the personal information businesses collect about them and requires businesses to inform consumers about how they collect, use, and retain their personal information.\n\nIn 2020, the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA), also known as Proposition 24, amended the CCPA by adding additional consumer privacy rights and obligations for businesses. It also established the California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) and tasked it with responsibilities including implementing and enforcing the law and educating the public on their rights and obligations under the law. The CPRA amended the CCPA; it did not create a separate, new law. The CPRA amendments to the CCPA went into effect on January 1, 2023.",

            "id": "1738",
            "name": "Australian Privacy Principles",
            "description": "The Australian Privacy Principles (APP) are the basis of the 1988 Australian Privacy Act, which was significantly amended in the year 2000.\n\nAPP is a privacy framework that applies to Australian government organizations, organizations that provide health services, and any private sector organization generating an annual revenue of over $3 million. This includes organizations outside Australia that store or process data of Australian citizens.\nThere are 13 privacy principles that set standards, rights and obligations, including:\n\n* The collection, disclosure, and usage of personal data\n* Governance and responsibilities requirements\n* Integrity of personal information\n* An individual’s right to access personal information\n\nThe Australian Privacy Principles are principles-based law. This gives an organisation or agency flexibility to tailor their personal information handling practices to their business models and the diverse needs of individuals. They are also technology neutral, which allows them to adapt to changing technologies.",

            "id": "304",

            "description": "This document specifies requirements and provides guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving a Privacy Information Management System (PIMS) in the form of an extension to ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27002 for privacy management within the context of the organization.\n\nThis document specifies PIMS-related requirements and provides guidance for PII controllers and PII processors holding responsibility and accountability for PII processing.\n\nThis document is applicable to all types and sizes of organizations, including public and private companies, government entities and not-for-profit organizations, which are PII controllers and/or PII processors processing PII within an ISMS.",

        {
            "id": "3846",
            "name": "EU DORA",
            "description": "The EU DORA requires financial entities to ensure digital operational resilience and implement an effective information and communication technology (ICT) risk management framework, mechanisms and policies for handling all ICT-related incidents, and for reporting major ICT-related incidents, testing of ICT systems, controls, and processes, as well as for managing ICT third-party risk. \n\n\n\nThe EU DORA applies to the following financial entities: \n\n(a) credit institutions, \n\n(b) payment institutions, including payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366 (Payment Services Directive), \n\n(c) account information service providers, \n\n(d) electronic money institutions, including electronic money institutions exempted pursuant to Directive 2009/110/EC (Taking up, pursuit and prudential supervision of the business of electronic money institutions amending Directives and repealing Directive); \n\n(e) investment firms; \n\n(f) crypto-asset service providers as authorised under a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on markets in crypto assets, and amending Regulations (EU) No 1093/2010 and (EU) No 1095/2010 and Directives 2013/36/EU and (EU) 2019/1937 (‘the Regulation on markets in crypto-assets’) and issuers of asset-referenced tokens; \n\n(g) central securities depositories; \n\n(h) central counterparties; \n\n(i) trading venues; \n\n(j) trade repositories; \n\n(k) managers of alternative investment funds; \n\n(l) management companies; \n\n(m) data reporting service providers; \n\n(n) insurance and reinsurance undertakings; \n\n(o) insurance intermediaries, reinsurance intermediaries and ancillary insurance intermediaries; \n\n(p) institutions for occupational retirement provision; \n\n(q) credit rating agencies; \n\n(r) administrators of critical benchmarks; \n\n(s) crowdfunding service providers; \n\n(t) securitisation repositories; \n\n(u) ICT third-party service providers. \n\n\n\nThe EU DORA does not apply to the following: \n\n(a) managers of alternative investment funds as referred to in Article 3(2) of Directive 2011/61/EU (Alternative Investment Fund Managers and amending Directives); \n\n(b) insurance and reinsurance undertakings as referred to in Article 4 of Directive 2009/138/EC (Taking-up and pursuit of the business of Insurance and Reinsurance Solvency II); \n\n(c) institutions for occupational retirement provision which operate pension schemes which together do not have more than 15 members in total; \n\n(d) natural or legal persons exempted pursuant to Articles 2 and 3 of Directive 2014/65/EU (Markets in financial instruments and amending Directive); \n\n(e) insurance intermediaries, reinsurance intermediaries and ancillary insurance intermediaries which are microenterprises or small or medium-sized enterprises; \n\n(f) post office giro institutions as referred to in Article 2(5), point (3), of Directive 2013/36/EU (Access to the activity of credit institutions and the prudential supervision of credit institutions and investment firms)",

            "id": "3927",
            "name": "Colorado AI Act",
            "description": "The Colorado AI Act focuses on the development and deployment of “high-risk” AI systems and their potential to cause algorithmic discrimination. It creates duties for developers and deployers to use reasonable care to avoid algorithmic discrimination via high-risk AI systems. \n\nAlgorithmic discrimination is defined as any condition in which the use of an AI system results in an unlawful differential treatment or impact that disfavors an individual or group of individuals on the basis of their actual or perceived age, color, disability, ethnicity, genetic information, limited proficiency in the English language, national origin, race, religion, reproductive health, sex, veteran status or other classification protected under the laws of Colorado or federal law.\n\nA “high-risk” AI system is defined as any system that, when deployed, makes or is a substantial factor in making a “consequential decision”; namely, a decision that has a material effect on the provision or cost of:\n\n* education enrollment or an education opportunity,\n* employment or an employment opportunity,\n* a financial or lending service,\n* an essential government service,\n* health care services,\n* housing,\n* insurance, or\n* a legal service.\n\nThe law contains general duties for both deployers and developers of high-risk AI systems. \n\n* A “developer” refers to an individual or entity doing business in Colorado that develops or intentionally and substantially modifies a high-risk AI system. \n* A “deployer” refers to an individual or entity doing business in Colorado that deploys a high-risk AI system.\n\nDeployers that meet the following criteria are exempt from the law, other than the requirement to notify consumers that a consequential decision was made about them using a high-risk AI system:\n\n* The deployer employs less than 50 people.\n* The deployer does not use its own data to train the system.\n* The system deployed is used for its intended purpose (as specified by the developer and required under the law).\n* The deployer makes available to consumers the impact assessment provided by the developer.\n\nThere are also exemptions for systems that have been approved by a federal agency, entities subject to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act and certain other entities that are subject to existing laws and regulations.\n\nThe law will go into effect on 1 February 2026.",

            "id": "4125",
            "name": "CN PIPL",
            "description": "The Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) of China, enacted to safeguard personal information rights, regulates how personal information is processed, ensuring that data privacy is protected within China. It came into force on November 1, 2021.\n\nThe PIPL applies to:\n\n# *Personal Information Processors*: Organizations or individuals that determine the purposes and methods of personal information processing.\n# *Territorial Application*: It applies to the processing of personal information within China and, in specific circumstances, to the processing outside China involving individuals within its territory. Such circumstances include offering products or services to individuals in China, analyzing or evaluating behaviors within China, and other instances prescribed by law.\n\nCertain activities, like processing for household purposes or under other specific laws, are exempt from the PIPL.\n\nThe Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) is responsible for enforcing the PIPL. \n\nViolations may result in fines up to RMB 50 million or 5% of annual turnover, penalties for individuals up to RMB 1 million, business suspension, permit revocation, and public disclosure of offenses.",

            "description": "The Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) is a legislative framework in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA) that regulates the processing of personal data. It has been effective since September 14, 2023, and applies to entities inside KSA and to foreign entities processing personal data of individuals residing in KSA. This includes data of the deceased if it can identify them or a family member.             "name": "RIIO-3 Data Best Practice Guidance",
            "description": "The [RIIO-3 Data Best Practice Guidance|https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2025-06/Data-Best-Practice-Guidance-v3.5.pdf] is a core component of the Digitalisation Licence Condition applicable to network operators regulated under the RIIO-3 framework.
